title: Contributions of Small Mammals and Primates to Human‐Wildlife Conflict and Mitigation Measures Around Forest Fragments in Eastern Kenya
content:
ABSTRACT

Human-wildlife conflict (HWC) is a rising threat to food security, particularly among households located near protected areas (PAs). This study documented patterns of HWC involving small mammals and primates in three forest patches in Embu County, Kenya. Data were collected using structured questionnaires administered to 300 smallholder farmers (100 per forest patch) and through Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with farmers and Community Forest Association (CFA) members. Vervet monkeys were the leading crop raiders in Maranga and Kirimiri (18.7% and 16.8%), while yellow baboons were the primary species involved in livestock predation in Maranga and Njukiri (24.8% and 36%). Common preventive measures employed by farmers included shouting, beating drums, chasing wildlife away, and applying mud to maize cobs, among others. To mitigate HWC, the planting of indigenous trees and wild fruit species within forest patches should be encouraged. Furthermore, improving community-based conflict mitigation and farmer training programmes might also help minimise losses from small mammals and primates.
